drills.q: True or false: a test with no assertions can still achieve 100% line coverage on the code it executes.
drills.a: True -- coverage only tracks execution, not whether the test checked anything about the result. This is Martin Fowler's 'Assertion-Free Testing' anti-pattern.

drills.q: What does it mean for a mutant to 'survive' mutation testing?
drills.a: Every test in the suite still passed despite the mutation changing the code's actual behavior -- meaning a real, deliberate behavior change went completely undetected, the exact shape of an unnoticed regression.

drills.q: Name the three mutation testing tools for Python, JVM, and JS/TS respectively.
drills.a: mutmut (Python), PIT/pitest (JVM: Java, Kotlin), Stryker/StrykerJS (JavaScript/TypeScript; Stryker.NET for C#).

drills.q: A team wants to gate merges at a 100% mutation score. What's wrong with this target, mechanically?
drills.a: Equivalent mutants -- mutations that are syntactically different but behaviorally identical to the original code under every input -- can never be killed by any test, so 100% is an unreachable target in any non-trivial codebase; chasing it wastes engineering effort or pressures people into contorting code just to eliminate equivalent mutants.

drills.q: Why is full mutation testing expensive, mechanically, and what's the rough cost multiplier?
drills.a: Each mutant requires a full rerun of the relevant test suite to classify kill/survive, and a modest codebase can generate hundreds to thousands of mutants -- naive full runs commonly cost 10-100x the underlying test suite's own runtime.

drills.q: A team mandates an 80% mutation-score CI gate on day one against a legacy codebase with historically weak tests. Predict the failure mode.
drills.a: Recreates the same Goodhart's-Law dynamic that broke coverage-as-a-target: intense pressure to satisfy the gate quickly produces either blocked PRs on unrelated pre-existing debt or superficial tests written specifically to kill mutants rather than genuinely verify behavior. PIT's guidance is to start around 70% and ratchet up as the suite genuinely improves.

drills.q: How does PIT use existing coverage data as a cost optimization before running mutants?
drills.a: It skips placing mutants on lines with zero test coverage, since a mutant there would trivially survive (no test reaches it) -- that outcome is already known from a plain coverage report, so PIT avoids wasting a full test-suite rerun confirming a certain result.

drills.q: Explain how StrykerJS's --incremental mode changes mutation testing's practical cost profile, with the reported numbers.
drills.a: It caches the previous run's mutant results in reports/stryker-incremental.json and only re-mutates/re-tests code changed since the last run, rather than the whole codebase. Reported real-world improvement: roughly 30 minutes down to under 2 minutes on typical PR-sized diffs -- the difference between mutation testing being a nightly-only batch job and living inside PR-gated CI.

drills.q: A mutant flips `age >= 18` to `age > 18` and survives. Diagnose the specific test gap, and explain why adding more non-boundary tests would not fix it.
drills.a: No existing test case exercises the exact boundary value age == 18 -- every test is either strictly above 18 (both operators agree) or strictly below (both agree). Only a test asserting the expected classification at exactly 18 can kill this mutant, because that's the only input where >= and > diverge; coverage of the line was already 100%, so more non-boundary tests add nothing to killing this specific mutant.

drills.q: Design a mutation testing rollout for a team that has 85% line coverage they're proud of and has never run mutation testing before. What do you tell them first, and what do you NOT do?
drills.a: Reset expectations: 85% line coverage says nothing about assertion quality, and surviving mutants in 'covered' code should be treated as new information, not a failure of the existing number. Scope the first run to one business-critical module, treat survivors as a small actionable backlog, and run it as a visibility tool for several cycles BEFORE gating any PR on a threshold -- don't run full-codebase mutation on day one and don't gate merges immediately.

drills.q: How would you decide which modules in a large codebase are worth the cost of mutation testing at all?
drills.a: Scope by regression cost and change frequency, not codebase size: modules where a silent behavior regression is expensive (billing, auth, anything touching money or access control) and modules with high churn are highest value. Stable, rarely-changed utility/glue code with minimal business logic is a poor use of the expensive per-mutant test-rerun cost. If the highest-risk module also has the slowest test suite, invest in speeding up that suite first, since mutation cost is a direct multiple of test runtime.
